The mixed design approach (MDA) integrates radar and infrared stealth optimization for fighter intake and exhaust systems.
Physical optics (PO) and physical theory of diffraction (PTD) are used to calculate radar cross section (RCS).
Monte Carlo and ray tracing methods are applied to evaluate infrared radiation intensity.
The aircraft model includes parameters such as air inlet model, exhaust model, nozzle stages, and baffle configurations.
The standard k–ε turbulence model is used for aerodynamic flow field simulation.
The objective functions minimize mean RCS, tail RCS, and infrared radiation intensity simultaneously.
The intake and exhaust system geometry significantly affects electromagnetic scattering and infrared emissions.
Nozzle baffles (lower, center, lateral) help block direct radiation and reduce detectability.
The optimized model reduced mean RCS by about 1.84 dBm² and tail RCS by about 32.92 dBm² compared to the initial model.
Infrared radiation in the 3–5 μm band is notably higher than in other atmospheric windows.
Environmental radiation effects are included in infrared signature calculations using reverse Monte Carlo methods.
The azimuth (α) and elevation (β) angles define observation geometry for stealth evaluation.
The model uses high-precision unstructured grids with local mesh refinement for flow simulation.
The MDA balances aerodynamic performance with radar and infrared stealth requirements.
Validation shows the infrared radiation calculation method closely matches reference data with minor deviations.
The aircraft intake is symmetrically located under the nose with the nozzle center above the fuselage axis.
The study uses a full factorial design method to explore parameter influences on stealth performance.
The radar cross section is calculated considering both facet and edge scattering contributions.
The infrared radiation model accounts for high-temperature exhaust gas heating the nozzle inner walls.
The study emphasizes the need for integrated stealth design due to joint radar and infrared detection threats.
